messages.subject: Spatial abundance estimation of deer: combining kernel and
parts:
Hi everybody,

I am working on the last part of my PhD thesis on the ecology and
conservation of two brocket deer species (Mazama americana and M. pandora)
and white-tailed deer in the Yucatan Peninsula, Mexico (Greater Calakmul
Region). I would like to know your opinion on a new technique that I am
trying to develop.

Unfortunatelly, I am not a regular user of Distance sampling for the simple
reason that sightings of these animals in my study area are very
infrequent. For example, in four years of transect work (more that 1200 km
walked) for both direct (sightings) and indirect(tracks, pathways)surveys,
only 62 sightings with accurate information (e. g. correct species id,
perpendicular distances) were made. This does not mean that deer are not
abundant in the area as confirmed by relativelly high abundance indices (as
compared with other areas elsewhere in the Neotropics) and high harvest
rates by local subsistence hunters. Basically, the problem is that close
understory vegetation, high hunting pressure, difficulty in walking quietly
through the forest and overall waryness of deer preclude the use of
observations for abundance/density estimations.

I have been working on a model to predict the spatial abundance of deer in
this area with the combined use of kernel isophlets and transect surveys
with deer signs (tracks/patways)observations.

My survey design was the following:

The information on deer abundance comes from the 46 non-permanent transects
set in a random-stratified fashion over a large study area of about 155
km2. Deer abundance was estimated with the count of deer sign encounter
rates (SER =3D tracks/deer patways/km). During the monitoring of this
transects, sections of 100 meters were marked with flagging tape and
therefore a rough estimate of the exact location of each individual
detection event can be positioned within the length of the transect at 100
meters intervals. Only the transects with no overlapping sampling areas
were chosen for this analysis.

To accomplish this, the following 4 steps were necessary: (1) The exact
GPS location of the transect and its total length was incorporated into a
GIS line coverage. The habitat gradients that the transect crosses can be
estimated by overlaying the transect with the vegetation map of the study
area (2) The approximated location of deer SER detections events is
digitalized as a point coverage, overlaying the transect coverage using the
information on transect length and the 100 meters sections to pinpoint the
exact location of the detection events.


(3) Because the amount and spatial distribution of detection events can be
extremely variable within the transects in absolute numbers, a rating
system of SER location is used rather than exact numbers. This rating
system uses the following categories to group SER events into point
clusters: =A1=DC 1 deer signs/km =3D 1 point; between 1 to 2 deer signs/km =3D=
2
points; between 2 to 3 deer signs/km =3D 3 points and =A1=DD 4 deer signs/km=
=3D 5
points, (4) this rates are considered equivalent to very low, low, moderate
and high abundance of deer signs, respectively and therefore can be
interpreted as an spatial index of relative abundance, where (I argue)that
probabilistic Adaptive Kernel (AK) isophlets can also be estimated using
clustered deer sign groups rather than number of signs. It is argued that
this method provides an accurate picture of deer abundance at the landscape
level when mapped with the AK method in a GIS.

To calculate AK with this information, deer abundance was rated with a 95%
probability or 1 confidence interval (CI) that =A1=DD 5 SER/km will occur;
moderate deer abundance with a 90% probability or 2 CI for 2 to 3 SER/km;
low deer abundance with 85% probability or 3 CI for 2 SER/km and very low
deer abundance with an 80% probability or 5 CI for =A1=DC 1 SER/km. Finally,=
a
least square validation of the Kernel isophlets is performed and the map
can now be compared with the other methods used for deer abundance
estimation.

My hypthesis is that, the AK provide a spatial representation of the
probability of finding a given deer sign encounter rate per square
kilometre (SER/km2) in a landscape sampled with systematic, random,
stratified transects. This might be interpreted as an indirect method for
the estimation and spatial representation of the relative abundance of deer
in that sampled landscape.

The comparisons of abundance estimates with traditional SER methods and my
model are very similar with the advantage that I can now visualise the
spatial representation of abundance in my study area.

I have found a few references on the combined use of kernel and distance
methods, but all are completelly theoretical (Mack Y, P and Quang P, X.
1998. Kernel methods in line and point transect sampling. Biometrics. 54:
606-619. Mack, Y. P., Quang P. X. and Zhang, S 1999. Kernel estimation in
transect sampling without the shoulder condition. Communications in
statistics theory and methods. 28: 2277-2296). So far, I have been unable
to find any empirical study on the use of these two methods.

Now, my main questions for you guys in the list are three:

1. As I understand from the literature, a kernel estimate provides a direct
density estimate that can be interpreted as a Utilization Distribution
function. Is it "safe" to assume that the utilization distribution (UD)
estimate from Kernel methods provides and accurate spatial representation
of the abundance in this case and with this design?

2. I have been looking for methods to validate my model. Unfortunatelly I
have no abundance estimation other than SER, but I do have GPS locations of
deer kills by hunters (92 in total over the same four years period)that I
am using to estimate the spatial and temporal patterns of deer hunters. Can
you think of a way where I can compare these two independent data-sets to
validate my kernel-transect model?

3. Is there anybody out there that you may know who might have used kernel-
tansect methods in a similar fashion?

Thanks a lot for your input and sorry for the long message.
Regards

Manuel
